Tell the children to cross out each word once they have used it.
3:root-words-in-context.stuck: Read the sentence to the child once with each of the words that are left and ask which one sounds right. The child starts with the sentences they are sure about; the last word goes in the last gap. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the words are, in order, joyfully, enjoy, enjoyment, joyful, then sleeper, sleepy, sleepiness, sleepily.

3:column-regrouping.say: "These are addition problems with three-digit numbers, written one number under the other. Add one place at a time, starting with the ones. When a place adds up to ten or more, regroup: write the ones digit of that sum and carry the 1 to the next place."
3:column-regrouping.first: Write the first problem on the board the way it is printed: 261 plus 285. Add the ones: 1 plus 5 is 6. Add the tens: 6 plus 8 is 14, so write 4 under the tens and carry the 1 into the small box above the hundreds. Add the hundreds: 2 plus 2 plus the carried 1 is 5. Read the whole answer aloud: 546. Point out that the small boxes above each problem are for the carried digits.
3:column-regrouping.stuck: Have the child cover all but one column and say its sum aloud. If the sum is ten or more, ask, "Which digit stays here, and which digit is carried?" The most common slip is to forget the carried 1; the child checks the small box before adding the next column. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 546, 521, 708, 909, 889, and 703.

G3-359.say: "These are addition problems, written one number under the other. Add one place at a time, starting with the ones. When a place adds up to ten or more, regroup: write the ones digit of that sum and carry the 1 to the next place."
G3-359.first: Write the second problem on the board the way it is printed: 18 plus 55. Add the ones: 8 plus 5 is 13, so write 3 under the ones and carry the 1 into the small box above the tens. Add the tens: 1 plus 5 plus the carried 1 is 7. Read the whole answer aloud: 73. Tell the children that in some problems the tens add up to ten or more; then the answer has three digits.
G3-359.stuck: Have the child cover all but one column and say its sum aloud. If the sum is ten or more, ask, "Which digit stays here, and which digit is carried?" The child checks the small box before adding the next column. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 149, 73, 123, 134, 117, and 54.

G3-360.say: "These are subtraction problems, written one number under the other. Subtract one place at a time, starting with the ones. When the top digit is too small, regroup: take one ten from the tens place and turn it into ten ones."
G3-360.first: Write the first problem on the board the way it is printed: 73 minus 17. Look at the ones: "3 minus 7. Can we do that?" No, so regroup: cross out the 7 tens and write 6, and turn the 3 ones into 13. Now 13 minus 7 is 6, and 6 tens minus 1 ten is 5 tens. Read the whole answer aloud: 56.
G3-360.stuck: Have the child ask at the ones place, "Is the top digit big enough?" If not, the child crosses out the tens digit, writes one less above it, and puts a small 1 in front of the ones digit. The most common slip is to subtract the smaller digit from the bigger one no matter which is on top. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 56, 37, 19, 36, 27, and 48.

G3-357@w.say: "Look at the sign of each problem first. Work one place at a time, starting with the ones: carry when a sum is ten or more, borrow when the top digit is too small."
G3-357@w.first: Write the first problem on the board, one number under the other. Point to the sign first. Work the ones column first: if it is 10 or more, carry a ten; if you cannot take away, borrow a ten. Then the tens and the hundreds.
G3-357@w.stuck: Have the child cover all but one column and work it aloud. If a sum is ten or more, carry the ten; if the top digit is too small, borrow a ten. Check the sign of each problem first.

G3-362@w.say: "These are subtraction problems, written one number under the other. Work one place at a time, starting with the ones, and borrow when the top digit is too small. Where the tens digit is 0, borrow from the hundreds first."
G3-362@w.first: Write the first problem on the board. The top number has a zero in the tens place, so to borrow for the ones you first borrow from the hundreds: the 0 becomes 10, then 9. Work it through together.
G3-362@w.stuck: Have the child work one column at a time. Where the tens digit is 0, the child borrows from the hundreds first: the 0 becomes 10, then gives one ten to the ones and becomes 9.

G3-363@w.say: "Look at the sign of each problem first: some add and some take away. Work one place at a time, starting with the ones: carry when a sum is ten or more, borrow when the top digit is too small."
G3-363@w.first: Write the first problem on the board, one number under the other. Point to the sign first: the page mixes adding and taking away. Work the ones column first and carry or borrow when you need to.
G3-363@w.stuck: Have the child cover all but one column and work it aloud. If a sum is ten or more, carry the ten; if the top digit is too small, borrow a ten. Check the sign of each problem first.

3:mult-div-relationship.say: "Multiplication and division belong together. One array gives a whole family of four facts: two multiplications and two divisions. Use each array to finish all four number sentences next to it."
3:mult-div-relationship.first: Draw the first array on the board: 2 rows of 5. Count the rows and count how many are in one row. Finish the two multiplications: 2 times 5 is 10, and 5 times 2 is 10. Then ask, "Ten shapes in 2 equal rows: how many are in each row?" Finish the two divisions: 10 divided by 2 is 5, and 10 divided by 5 is 2. Show that all four facts use the same three numbers.
3:mult-div-relationship.stuck: Have the child count the rows, the shapes in one row, and all the shapes, and write these three numbers next to the array. Every number sentence of the family uses only these three numbers. For a division, ask, "How many groups of 5 can you see in the array?" For your own reference, on the page for everyone the four arrays hold 10, 30, 15, and 12 shapes.

G3-312@w.say: "Count the rows of each array and the things in one row. Write the missing factor."
G3-312@w.first: Draw an array on the board, for example 2 rows of 7. Write ? × 7 = 14 and ask, "How many rows of 7 make 14?" Count the rows together. Do the first one on the page together.
G3-312@w.stuck: Have the child count the rows and the shapes in one row of the array. The missing factor is the number that is not printed: rows times shapes in a row makes the total.

G3-369@w.say: "Use the three numbers on the roof of each house to finish two multiplications and two divisions."
G3-369@w.first: Draw a house with 2, 9, and 18 on the roof. Write the four facts together: 2 × 9, 9 × 2, 18 ÷ 2, 18 ÷ 9. The biggest number is the product. Do the first house on the page together.
G3-369@w.stuck: Have the child find the biggest number on the roof: it is the product. The two smaller numbers are the factors: they multiply to the product, and the product divided by one factor gives the other.

3:magic-squares.say: "In a magic square, every row and every column adds up to the same number: the magic number. On this page the magic number is 15. Fill in the empty cells so that every row and every column adds up to 15."
3:magic-squares.first: Draw the first square on the board. Find a row or a column with only one empty cell: the top row has 6 and 1. Ask, "6 and 1 make 7. How many more do we need to get to 15?" Write 8 in the empty cell. Tell the children to look for a row or a column with just one empty cell each time; every number they fill in opens up the next one.
3:magic-squares.stuck: Have the child run a finger along a row or a column with one empty cell, add the two numbers that are there, and count up to 15. To check a finished square, the child adds every row and every column. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the rows of the first square are 6, 1, 8, then 7, 5, 3, then 2, 9, 4; the rows of the second square are 6, 7, 2, then 1, 5, 9, then 8, 3, 4.

3:input-output.say: "Each number machine has a rule, printed at the top. A number goes in on the left, the machine uses its rule, and a new number comes out on the right. Fill in the missing numbers. Watch out: sometimes the number that went in is the one that is missing."
3:input-output.first: Do the first machine together. Its rule is plus 7. Ask, "14 goes in. What comes out?" Write 21. Then do the row where the box on the left is empty: "Something went in, the machine added 7, and 22 came out. What went in?" Work backward: 22 minus 7 is 15. Check it by putting 15 through the machine.
3:input-output.stuck: Ask the child, "Is the missing number before the arrow or after it?" After the arrow, the child uses the rule. Before the arrow, the child does the opposite and subtracts, then checks by putting the number through the machine. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the first machine gives 21, 24, 15, and 44; the second gives 37, 14, 36, and 4.

G3-328+.say: "Each number machine has a rule, printed at the top. A number goes in on the left, the machine uses its rule, and a new number comes out on the right. One machine multiplies, and one subtracts. Fill in the missing numbers. Watch out: sometimes the number that went in is the one that is missing."
G3-328+.first: Do the first machine together. Its rule is times 5. Ask, "6 goes in. What comes out?" Write 30. Then do the row where the box on the left is empty: "Something went in, the machine multiplied it by 5, and 35 came out. What went in?" Work backward: 35 divided by 5 is 7. Check it by putting 7 through the machine.
G3-328+.stuck: Ask the child, "Is the missing number before the arrow or after it?" After the arrow, the child uses the rule. Before the arrow, the child does the opposite (divide for times, add for minus) and then checks by putting the number through the machine. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the first machine gives 30, 60, 7, 50, and 2; the second gives 18, 15, 7, 27, and 9.

G3-328@w.first: Read the rule of the first machine aloud, for example "+9." Do the first number together: put it in, use the rule, and write what comes out. If the number that comes out is given, go backward: use the opposite rule.
G3-328@w.stuck: Ask the child, "Is the missing number before the arrow or after it?" After the arrow, the child uses the rule. Before the arrow, the child does the opposite, then checks by putting the number through the machine.

3:person-words.say: "Many words for people are made from a verb and an ending. Someone who teaches is a teacher. Look at each person, read the word next to them, and write the word for the person who does it in the empty brick."
3:person-words.first: Do the first two on the board. Ask, "Someone who runs is a …?" Write runner and point out the double n. Ask, "Someone who takes photographs is a …?" Write photographer. Tell the children that every person word on this page ends in -er.
3:person-words.stuck: Have the child say the sentence aloud: "Someone who ___ is a ___." For the spelling: a word that ends in e only adds an r, as in dance and dancer; run doubles its last letter. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the words are runner, photographer, dancer, gardener, teacher, baker, farmer, and singer.

3:area-model.say: "Each rectangle on this page is made of squares. The number of squares is the area of the rectangle. Count the rows, and count how many squares are in one row. Then finish the multiplication to find how many squares there are in all."
3:area-model.first: Draw the first rectangle on the board: 3 rows of 5 squares. Count the rows, then count the squares in one row. Say, "3 rows of 5: 3 times 5 is 15." Count the squares one by one to check. Say the answer as a sentence: "The area is 15 squares."
3:area-model.stuck: Have the child run a finger down the left side to count the rows and along the top to count the squares in one row. A child who does not know the fact adds the rows, 5 plus 5 plus 5, or counts every square. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 15, 16, 20, and 27.

G3-488@w.say: "To find the area of a rectangle, multiply its two side lengths. Write the equation and the area with its unit."
G3-488@w.first: Draw a rectangle on the board with sides 4 and 3 and fill it with a grid: count the squares, 12. Show that 4 × 3 = 12 square units. Do the first rectangle on the page together and write the unit.
G3-488@w.stuck: Have the child find the two side lengths and multiply them. A child who does not know the fact adds one side as many times as the other side says. The unit is "square" and the unit of the sides.

G3-489@w.say: "Draw one straight line to split each L-shape into two rectangles. Find the area of each part. Then add the two areas."
G3-489@w.first: Draw an L-shape on the board and split it with one line into two rectangles. Find each area and add them. Do the first shape on the page together.
G3-489@w.stuck: Help the child draw the line where the L bends, so that two rectangles show. Then find the two side lengths of each rectangle; a missing length is the long side take away the short side.

3:water-cycle.say: "This is a science page about the water cycle: the way water travels from the sea up into the sky and back down again. The diagram has four numbers. Read the four words in the bank, and write each word on the line that has the same number as its place in the diagram."
3:water-cycle.first: Follow the arrows in the diagram together, starting at the sea: the Sun warms the water and it rises into the air; high up it cools and forms a cloud; it falls as rain; it runs back to the sea. Read the four words aloud and say each one in plain words: evaporation means water rises into the air, condensation means it turns into the tiny drops of a cloud, precipitation means rain or snow falls, and collection means the water gathers in rivers, lakes, and the sea. Do number 1 together.
3:water-cycle.stuck: Point to the number in the diagram and ask, "What is the water doing here: going up, making a cloud, falling, or gathering?" Then read the four words to the child again. For your own reference, on the page for everyone 1 is evaporation, 2 is condensation, 3 is precipitation, and 4 is collection.

3:fraction-unit-build.say: "Each shape on this page is cut into equal parts, and some of the parts are shaded. Write the fraction that the shaded parts show. The bottom number tells how many equal parts the whole shape has. The top number tells how many of them are shaded."
3:fraction-unit-build.first: Draw the first shape on the board: a bar cut into four equal parts, with two of them shaded. Ask, "How many equal parts does the bar have in all?" Write 4 in the bottom box. Ask, "How many parts are shaded?" Write 2 in the top box. Read the fraction aloud: two fourths.
3:fraction-unit-build.stuck: Have the child count all the parts first, shaded or not, and write that number at the bottom; then the child counts only the shaded parts for the top. The most common slip is to count only the parts that are not shaded for the bottom number.

G3-316@w.first: Draw a rectangle cut into four equal parts and color three: "three fourths." Do the first shape on the page together: read the fraction, count the equal parts, and color as many as the top number says.
G3-316@w.say: "Each shape is cut into equal parts. Read the fraction next to it and color that many parts: the top number tells how many to color, the bottom number how many equal parts the whole has."
G3-316@w.stuck: Have the child count the equal parts of the shape and check them against the bottom number. Then color one part at a time, counting up to the top number.

3:perimeter.say: "The perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape, like a walk along its edge. Each rectangle on this page is made of squares. Count the edges of the small squares all the way around the outside of the rectangle. Write the perimeter in the box."
3:perimeter.first: Draw the first rectangle on the board. Mark a starting corner with a dot. Count the edges along the top, down the side, along the bottom, and back up to the dot, making a small mark on each edge as you count it. Write the total in the box. Then show the shortcut: count each of the four sides and add the four numbers.
3:perimeter.stuck: Have the child mark a starting corner and make a small mark on each edge as it is counted, so that no edge is skipped or counted twice. A child who counts the squares inside is finding the area; point to the outside edge. A square in a corner has two outside edges, and both count. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the perimeters are 20, 14, 20, and 22.

G3-490@w.say: "The perimeter of each shape is given. Write an equation with n for the missing side. Then find n."
G3-490@w.first: Draw a rectangle on the board with sides 5, 5, 10, and n and the perimeter 30. Add the sides you know (20) and ask, "What more makes 30?" n = 10. Do the first shape on the page together.
G3-490@w.stuck: Have the child add the sides that are given and take that sum away from the perimeter: what is left is n. Check by adding all the sides, n too: the sum must be the perimeter.

3:life-cycles-compare.say: "This is a science page about two animals that change a great deal as they grow: the butterfly and the frog. Read each sentence. If it is true for the butterfly, put a check under the butterfly. If it is true for the frog, put a check under the frog. If it is true for both, check both."
3:life-cycles-compare.first: Ask the children how each animal grows, and write the two chains on the board: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly; and egg, tadpole, young frog, frog. Do the first sentence together: "The grown-up catches insects to eat." That is true for the frog only, so only the frog gets a check. Tell the children that some sentences are true for both animals.
3:life-cycles-compare.stuck: Read the sentence to the child and ask about each animal separately: "Is that true for the butterfly? Is it true for the frog?" Point to the two chains on the board. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are, from top to bottom: frog, butterfly, both, frog, butterfly, frog, both, butterfly.

1:tens-and-ones.say: "Each picture shows a number built from tens and ones. The long rods are tens, and the small cubes are ones. Count the tens. Count the ones. Then write the number."
1:tens-and-ones.first: Do the first one on the board. Draw the rods as lines and the cubes as dots. Count the rods by tens together: 10, 20, 30, and so on. Then count on by ones for the cubes. Write the number and point to its digits: the tens digit tells how many rods, and the ones digit tells how many cubes.
1:tens-and-ones.stuck: Have the child touch each rod and count by tens, then touch each cube and keep counting by ones. A child who writes the digits in the wrong order says the number aloud first and then writes what they hear. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 99, 63, 51, and 41.

G1-563@w.say: "Each picture shows ten-rods. Each rod is ten. Count the tens, write how many tens there are, and then write the number."
G1-563@w.first: Draw three rods on the board and count by tens: "10, 20, 30. Three tens is thirty." Do the first one on the page together: count the rods, write the number of tens, then the number.
G1-563@w.stuck: Have the child touch each rod and count by tens: 10, 20, 30. The number of rods is the number of tens, and the number ends in 0.

G1-564@w.say: "Each picture shows one ten-rod and some ones. Write how many ones there are, and then write the number: ten and some more."
G1-564@w.first: Draw one rod and three small cubes on the board: "One ten and three ones: thirteen." Do the first one on the page together: count the ones, write the number of ones, then the number.
G1-564@w.stuck: Have the child say "ten" for the rod and count on by ones for each cube: eleven, twelve, thirteen. The number starts with 1 and ends with the number of ones.

2:family-relationships.say: "Now it is time to read and think. Each sentence is a riddle about Tom's family. Read the riddle and work it out step by step. Then write the right family word from the box on the line. You will use each word more than one time."
2:family-relationships.first: Read the four words in the box aloud together. Do the first riddle on the board in two steps, drawing a stick person for each step: "Tom's dad's mom. Start with Tom. Step one: Tom's dad. Step two: his dad's mom. What does Tom call his dad's mom?" Write grandma. Keep every example about Tom's family, not about the children's own families. Tell the children that some families use other names, such as Nana or Abuela; on this page they use the words in the box.
2:family-relationships.stuck: Have the child cover the end of the riddle and say who the first two words are ("Tom's mom"), then add the last word ("her brother"). A quick sketch of three stick people helps. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are grandma, uncle, grandma, aunt, grandpa, aunt, grandpa, and uncle.

G2-362@w.say: "Now it is time to read and think. Each sentence is a riddle about one child's family. Read the riddle and work it out step by step. Then write the right family word from the box on the line. Some words fit more than one riddle."
G2-362@w.first: Draw a family tree on the board with stick people: the child the riddles are about at the bottom; the mom and the dad above the child; a grandma and a grandpa above each parent; an aunt or an uncle beside each parent; and a cousin under the aunt. Read the first riddle aloud and follow it on the tree together, one step at a time, and write the word. Keep to the family on the page, not the children's own families.
G2-362@w.stuck: Have the child cover the end of the riddle and say who its first part names ("the dad"), then add the last word ("his brother"). Following the riddle on the tree on the board helps. The children of an aunt or an uncle are cousins.

2:logic-grid.say: "These are logic puzzles. In each puzzle three children each have one of the three pictures at the top of the grid, and no two children have the same one. The clues tell you what a child does NOT have. Put an X in the grid for every clue. When only one box is left in a row, that is what the child has."
2:logic-grid.first: Do the first puzzle together. Read the first clue aloud, find the child's row and the picture's column, and put an X in the box where they meet. Do the other two clues the same way. Then show the two rules: a row with two Xs gets a check mark in its last box, and a check mark puts an X in every other box of its row and its column, because each child has only one picture and only one child has each picture. The small grid at the top right of the page shows this: one check mark with Xs around it. When every row has a check mark, find each child's strip under the puzzle and circle the picture that child has. Children do the second puzzle on their own. Children who finish write one sentence for each child on the back ("Ben has the dog."), then make up a puzzle for a partner: three names, three pictures, and three "does not have" clues.
2:logic-grid.stuck: Have the child read one clue at a time and make its X before reading the next one. Then ask, "Which row has only one empty box? Which column?" A box that is the last one left in its row or in its column gets the check mark. For your own reference, on the page for everyone: in the first puzzle Ben has the dog, Mia the mouse, and Tom the cat; in the second puzzle Leo has the frog, Max the hamster, and Emma the turtle.

2:expanded-form-digit-value.say: "Every digit in a number is worth something. In 479, the 4 is worth 400, the 7 is worth 70, and the 9 is worth 9. This page goes both ways. When the parts are printed, put them together and write the number in the box. When the number is printed, break it into its hundreds, its tens, and its ones."
2:expanded-form-digit-value.first: Write 400 + 70 + 9 = on the board, as in problem 1. Ask, "How many hundreds? How many tens? How many ones?" and write 479. Then write 756 = with three empty boxes, as in problem 5. Read it aloud, "seven hundred fifty-six," and ask what each digit is worth: 700 + 50 + 6. Point to the 5 and say, "This 5 stands for 50, so 50 goes in the middle box." The easier page has only tens and ones; give it to everyone if the class has not worked with hundreds yet. On the page for early finishers, the parts are out of order and a place can be missing: 50 + 600 is 650.
2:expanded-form-digit-value.stuck: Have the child read the number aloud slowly and write what each part says: "two hundred" is 200, "forty" is 40, "two" is 2. A child who writes 2 + 4 + 2 for 242 has copied the digits; point to the first 2 and ask, "Is this 2 ones or 2 hundreds?" The usual order is hundreds, tens, ones; the right three parts in another order, such as 40 + 200 + 2, are still correct. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are, in the order of the problems, 479, 988, 926, 798, 700 + 50 + 6, 771, 200 + 40 + 2, 200 + 20 + 9, 800 + 40 + 5, and 800 + 30 + 3.

G2-401@w.first: Write 257 on the board and break it up together: 200 + 50 + 7. Then go the other way: 400 + 30 + 2 = 432. Point out that some problems put the parts together and others break the number up. Do the first one on the page together.
G2-401@w.stuck: Have the child read the number aloud slowly and write what each part says: "two hundred" is 200, "forty" is 40, "two" is 2. A child who writes 2 + 4 + 2 for 242 has copied the digits; point to the first 2 and ask, "Is this 2 ones or 2 hundreds?" The right three parts in another order are still correct.

K:animal-babies.say: "On the left are grown-up animals. On the right are their babies, but they are mixed up. Draw a line from each grown-up animal to its own baby."
K:animal-babies.first: Name the grown-up animals together, then the babies. Do the first one together: point to the first grown-up animal and ask, "Which baby belongs to it? How do you know?" Draw the line from dot to dot. Some babies look very different from their parents, like a caterpillar and a butterfly.
K:animal-babies.stuck: Point to one baby and ask what kind of animal it will be when it grows up. If the child does not know, say what the baby is called: a calf is a baby cow, a foal is a baby horse, a chick is a baby hen.

K:animal-groups-homes.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are two boxes for two kinds of animals. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
K:animal-groups-homes.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Where does this animal live? Does it live with people, or in the wild?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box.
K:animal-groups-homes.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? Where?" Then let the child choose the box.

K-204.first: Read the two boxes aloud, Pets and Wild Animals, and name every animal together. Do the first one together: ask, "Can this animal live in a house with people, or does it live in the wild?" Draw the line from the dot under it to its box. A rabbit can be a pet or wild; either box is right for it.

K-209.first: Read the two boxes aloud, Farm Animals and Wild Animals, and name every animal together. Do the first one together: ask, "Does this animal live on a farm, or in the wild?" Draw the line from the dot under it to its box.

K:articles.say: "Under each picture are two little words: a and an. Say the name of the picture with a in front of it, then with an. Circle the one that sounds right."
K:articles.first: Say the picture words of the page together first (they are below). Do the first one together: "a elephant, an elephant. Which sounds right?" Circle an. Tell the children that an goes in front of words that start with a, e, i, o, or u.
K:articles.stuck: Say both choices for the child, slowly, and let the child hear which one is easier to say. Ask, "Does the word start with a, e, i, o, or u?"

articles-animals-k306.first: Name the pictures together: elephant, pig, owl, fox. Do the first one together: "a elephant, an elephant. Which sounds right?" Circle an. Tell the children that an goes in front of words that start with a, e, i, o, or u. For your own reference: an elephant, a pig, an owl, a fox.

articles-food-bw-2-k306-2.first: Name the pictures together: donut, taco, egg, iron (the iron for clothes). Do the first one together: "a donut, an donut. Which sounds right?" Circle a. Tell the children that an goes in front of words that start with a, e, i, o, or u. For your own reference: a donut, a taco, an egg, an iron.

articles-household-bw-k306-4.first: Name the pictures together: cup, bed, umbrella, bottle. Do the first one together: "a cup, an cup. Which sounds right?" Circle a. Tell the children that an goes in front of words that start with a, e, i, o, or u. For your own reference: a cup, a bed, an umbrella, a bottle.

K:capital-letter.say: "Each box has the same sentence two times. One starts with a capital letter, and one does not. Circle the sentence that starts the right way. Then write that capital letter in the box."
K:capital-letter.first: Read the two sentences of the first box aloud while you point to them. Ask, "Which one starts with a big letter, a capital?" Circle it together and copy the capital letter into the box. Remind the children that every sentence starts with a capital letter.
K:capital-letter.stuck: Cover all but the first letter of each sentence with your finger and ask, "Which one is the big letter?" A child who is not sure may look for the same letter on the classroom alphabet.

K:conservation.say: "In each box there are two groups. Count each group and write how many. Then circle the check mark if the two groups have the same number, or the X if they do not."
K:conservation.first: Do the first box together: count the top group aloud, touching each picture, and write the number. Count the bottom group the same way. Ask, "Are the numbers the same?" Circle the check mark or the X. Tell the children that a group that is spread out can still have the same number as a group that is close together.
K:conservation.stuck: Have the child put a small dot on each picture while counting it, so that none is counted twice. Then compare the two numbers on the page: "Are they the same number?"

K:count-on.say: "The number on each box tells how many are hidden inside. Start at that number and count on, one more for each picture next to the box. Write how many there are in all."
K:count-on.first: Do the first one together: put your hand on the box and say its number. Then touch each picture and count on aloud: "Six… seven." Write the number in the empty box. Tell the children not to count the box from one: they start at its number.
K:count-on.stuck: Have the child say the number on the box and then tap each picture while saying the next number. If the child starts again at one, say the box number together and go on from there.

K:day-night.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are two boxes, Day and Night. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
K:day-night.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Do we see this in the day or at night?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. Some things can be seen in the day and at night, like the moon; let the child choose and say why.
K:day-night.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? Where?" Then let the child choose the box.

K:digraphs-k.say: "Two letters can make one sound. S and h say sh, like in shoe. C and h say ch, like in cheese. Say the name of each picture. Do you hear sh or ch? Draw a line to that side."
K:digraphs-k.first: Say sh and ch together a few times. Name the pictures together, so that everyone uses the same words. Do the first one together: say the word slowly and ask, "Do you hear sh or ch?" Draw the line to that side of the page.
K:digraphs-k.stuck: Say the word and stretch its first sound: "sh-sh-shoe." Then say "sh" and "ch" and ask which one it sounds like.

digraphs-k378.first: Say sh and ch together a few times. Name the pictures together: chocolate, shorts, wheelchair, cheese, shoe, shrimp. Do the first one together: say "chocolate" slowly and ask, "Do you hear sh or ch?" Draw the line to ch. For your own reference: ch: chocolate, wheelchair (the ch is in "chair"), cheese; sh: shorts, shoe, shrimp.

K:draw-shapes.say: "Each box names a shape. Connect the dots with your pencil to draw that shape. If there is a thick line in the box, start there."
K:draw-shapes.first: Read the name in each box aloud and draw that shape on the board: a triangle has 3 sides, a square has 4 sides that are all the same length, a rectangle has 4 sides with two long and two short. Draw the first shape together on the dot paper, going from dot to dot with straight lines.
K:draw-shapes.stuck: Have the child count the sides of the shape on the board and put a finger on the dots where the corners will go. Then draw one side at a time from corner to corner.

K:fruit-vegetable.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are two boxes, Fruits and Vegetables. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
K:fruit-vegetable.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Is this a fruit or a vegetable?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. If a food can be called both, either box is right when the child can say why.
K:fruit-vegetable.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? Where?" Then let the child choose the box.

K:healthy-food.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are two boxes, Healthy and Not Healthy. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
K:healthy-food.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Is this good for our body every day, or is it a treat for once in a while?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. A treat is fine once in a while; the page only asks which foods to eat every day.
K:healthy-food.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? Where?" Then let the child choose the box.

K:human-body.say: "Look at the picture. Each line points to a part of the body. The words are in the box at the top. Copy the right word onto each line."
K:human-body.first: Read the words in the box aloud and have the children touch that part of their own body for each one. Do the first line together: follow it with your finger to the part it points to, say its name, find the word in the box, and copy it onto the line letter by letter.
K:human-body.stuck: Have the child touch the part on their own body and say its name. Then find the word in the box together; the first letter helps: "Eye starts with e. Where is the word that starts with e?" Eye and ear both start with e: eye ends with e, ear ends with r.

K-344.say: "This page is about your face. Each line points to a part of the face. Copy the right word from the box onto each line. Then draw your own face in the big box."

human-body-k354-2.stuck: Have the child touch the part on their own body and say its name. Then find the word in the box together; the first letter helps: "Hand starts with h. Where is the word that starts with h?"

K:living-nonliving.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are two boxes, Living and Non-living. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
K:living-nonliving.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Does it grow and need water and air? Then it is living." Plants are living too, even though they do not walk or run. Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box.
K:living-nonliving.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? Where?" Then let the child choose the box.

K:naming-and-action-words.say: "Each row has three words. One of them is something you can DO, like hop or run. That is the action word. Circle it."
K:naming-and-action-words.first: Read the three words of the first row aloud and have the class read them with you: hop, egg, hat. Ask, "Which one can you do?" Have everyone hop once. Circle hop. Read each row aloud with the class before they choose.
K:naming-and-action-words.stuck: Read the three words for the child and ask about each one: "Can you ___?" The word that makes sense is the action word.

K:natural-made.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are two boxes, Natural and Man-made. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
K:natural-made.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Did people make this, or is it found in nature?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box.
K:natural-made.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? Where?" Then let the child choose the box.

K:one-more-one-less.say: "In each row, count the pictures. Then read the label. For one more, draw one more picture in the empty box. Write how many there are now."
K:one-more-one-less.first: Read the first label aloud: "1 more." Count the pictures together, then draw one more in the empty box (a circle is fine). Count again and write the new number after the arrow. Tell the children that one more is always the next number when we count.
K:one-more-one-less.stuck: Have the child count the pictures and then say the next number: "Four… then five." That is how many there are with one more.

K:period-or-question-mark.say: "Some sentences tell us something. Some sentences ask us something. A telling sentence ends with a period. An asking sentence ends with a question mark. Write the right mark in each box."
K:period-or-question-mark.first: Draw a period and a question mark on the board. Read the first sentence aloud: "The car is green." Ask, "Does it tell or ask?" It tells, so write a period. Read every sentence aloud to the class and let them decide before they write.
K:period-or-question-mark.stuck: Read the sentence again and ask, "Could you answer it with yes or no?" If you can, it asks, and it gets a question mark.

K:place-words.say: "Look at each picture. Where is the small picture? Circle the word that fits in the sentence."
K:place-words.first: Read the first sentence aloud with a hum for the gap: "The apple is hmm the circle." Read the three words below it. Ask, "Where is the apple?" Read the sentence with each word and circle the one that is true.
K:place-words.stuck: Have the child show the place word with a pencil and a book: "Put the pencil under the book. Now next to it." Then look at the picture again.

K:scene-search.say: "Look at the picture in the box at the top. Find every picture on the page that is just like it, and circle them all."
K:scene-search.first: Point to the picture in the box and name it together. Find one like it on the page together and circle it. Tell the children to look across the page row by row, like reading, so they do not miss any.
K:scene-search.stuck: Have the child cover the page with a sheet of paper and slide it down slowly, looking at one row at a time.

K-371.say: "Each picture is something we see every day. Is its shape a circle or a rectangle? Color the shape it has."
K-371.first: Draw a circle and a rectangle on the board and name them. Name the first picture together and ask, "Is it round like a circle, or does it have four sides like a rectangle?" Color that shape in the box next to the picture.
K-371.stuck: Have the child trace the outside of the picture with a finger: round all the way around is a circle; four straight sides are a rectangle.

K:shadow-closure.say: "Each picture on the left has a shadow on the right. A shadow is dark and shows only the shape. Draw a line from each picture to its shadow."
K:shadow-closure.first: Do the first one together: look at the outline of the first picture and ask, "Which shadow has the same shape?" Draw the line from dot to dot. Tell the children to look at the edges: the ears, the wheels, the tail.
K:shadow-closure.stuck: Have the child trace the outside of the picture with a finger, then trace the shadows until one has the same shape.

K-069.say: "In each row only a small part of a picture is showing. Which whole picture does it belong to? Circle it."
K-069.first: Do the first row together: look at the small part and ask, "What could this be? An ear, a tail, a head?" Look at the three whole pictures and circle the one the part belongs to.
K-069.stuck: Have the child find the part on each of the three pictures: "Does this one have it?"

K:singular-plural.say: "One means just one thing. Many means more than one. The word for one is written for you. Trace the word for many."
K:singular-plural.first: Read the first word aloud and show one finger. Then show two fingers and say the word for many. Point to the s at the end: "We add s when there is more than one." Trace the word for many together. Read each word on the page aloud with the class before they trace.
K:singular-plural.stuck: Read the word for one and the word for many for the child and have the child point to the part that is different. Then trace one letter at a time.

K-287.say: "The word for one is written for you. Read it with me. Then trace the word for many, and write it yourself on the empty line."

singular-plural-animals-k302.stuck: Read the word for one and the word for many for the child and have the child point to the part that is different. "Fox" gets -es: foxes. Then trace one letter at a time.

singular-plural-sea-life-bw-2-k287-2.stuck: Read the word for one and the word for many for the child and have the child point to the part that is different. "Octopus" gets -es: octopuses. Then trace one letter at a time.

K:subitize.say: "Look at each group very quickly, without counting one by one. How many do you see? Circle the number."
K:subitize.first: Hold up three fingers for a second and hide them: "How many?" Do the same with five. Then look at the first group on the page together for a moment and circle the number. Tell the children that it is fine to check by counting after they have guessed.
K:subitize.stuck: Have the child look for small groups inside the big one: "I see two and two. That makes four." Then count to check.

K:take-away.say: "Count the dots in each ten-frame. Some dots are crossed out: they are taken away. Write how many are left."
K:take-away.first: Do the first one together: count all the dots, then count the crossed-out ones. Read the number sentence aloud: "Ten take away one." Count the dots that are not crossed out and write the number after the equals sign.
K:take-away.stuck: Have the child cover each crossed-out dot with a finger and count only the dots that can still be seen.

K:teen-numbers.say: "A teen number is ten and some more. One ten-frame holds ten. Count what is in the two ten-frames and write the number. Then finish the number sentence: ten plus how many more."
K:teen-numbers.first: Do the first one together: point to the full ten-frame and say, "That is ten." Count on with the second frame: "eleven, twelve…" Write the number. Then read the sentence: "Twelve equals ten plus…" and write how many are in the second frame.
K:teen-numbers.stuck: Have the child start at ten for the full frame and count on, touching each dot in the second frame.

K-637.say: "Read the number in each row. Draw that many dots in the two ten-frames. Fill the first ten-frame all the way before you start the second one."
K-637.first: Do the first one together: read the number, for example 13. Fill the first ten-frame with ten dots while counting aloud, then count on in the second frame: "eleven, twelve, thirteen." Stop when you reach the number.
K-637.stuck: Have the child fill the first frame and say "ten", then draw one dot at a time in the second frame while counting on.

K:transport-flying.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are labeled boxes. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
K:transport-flying.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Where does this go? Does it fly?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box.
K:transport-flying.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? Where?" Then let the child choose the box.

1:add-three-addends.say: "Each problem adds three numbers. Look for two numbers that make ten, add them first, and then add the third number."
1:add-three-addends.first: Write 9 + 1 + 8 on the board. Ask, "Which two numbers make ten?" Circle 9 and 1: "Ten. Ten and eight more is eighteen." Write 18. Tell the children that if no two numbers make ten, they may add in any order.
1:add-three-addends.stuck: Have the child look at each pair of numbers and ask, "Do these two make ten?" If no pair does, add the first two, then count on the third with fingers.

G1-570.say: "Each story has three numbers. Read the story, draw it in the box, and write the three numbers in the number sentence. Look for two numbers that make ten. Then write how many in all."
G1-570.first: Read the first story aloud while the children follow. Ask, "What are the three numbers?" Write them on the board with plus signs. Draw quick circles for them. Look for two numbers that make ten together, add them first, then add the third.
G1-570.stuck: Read the story with the child, one sentence at a time, and underline each number. Have the child draw circles for each number and count them all.

1:animal-classes-coverings.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are boxes: Mammals, Birds, and Reptiles. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
1:animal-classes-coverings.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Does it have fur, feathers, or scales? Does it lay eggs or feed its babies milk?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. Mammals have fur or hair, birds have feathers, and reptiles have dry scales.
1:animal-classes-coverings.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? What is it like?" Then let the child choose the box.

G1-205.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are boxes: Fur, Feathers, and Scales. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
G1-205.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "What covers this animal's body: fur, feathers, or scales?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. Fur is soft hair, feathers have a stem with soft sides, and scales are small, hard plates on the skin.
G1-205.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? What is it like?" Then let the child choose the box.

1:blends-start.say: "Each word starts with two letters that you can hear together, like s and l in sled. Say the name of each picture. Write the two letters it starts with."
1:blends-start.first: Say "sled" slowly: "s-l-ed. Two sounds at the start: s and l." Name all the pictures together, so that everyone uses the same words (they are below). Do the first one together and write its two letters on the board.
1:blends-start.stuck: Say the word slowly and stretch the start: "ssslll-ed." Ask the child to say the first sound, then the second sound, and write both letters.

digraphs-g1493.first: Say "sled" slowly: "s-l-ed. Two sounds at the start: s and l." Name the pictures together: swan, train, sled, snail, spatula, stove, broom, flag. Do the first one together: "swan, s-w." Write sw. For your own reference: sw, tr, sl, sn, sp, st, br, fl.

digraphs-g1493-2.first: Say "sled" slowly: "s-l-ed. Two sounds at the start: s and l." Name the pictures together: dress, snowflake, flamingo, swing, stool, glass, slide, spatula. Do the first one together: "dress, d-r." Write dr. For your own reference: dr, sn, fl, sw, st, gl, sl, sp.

digraphs-g1493-3.first: Say "sled" slowly: "s-l-ed. Two sounds at the start: s and l." Name the pictures together: spider, dragon, flute, stove, crib, glove, plunger, snorkel. Do the first one together: "spider, s-p." Write sp. For your own reference: sp, dr, fl, st, cr, gl, pl, sn.

1:capitals-names-days-months.say: "Names of people and pets, and the days of the week, start with a capital letter. Other words do not, unless they start the sentence. In each sentence, circle the word that is written the right way."
1:capitals-names-days-months.first: Write "Monday" and "monday" on the board and ask which is right. Read the first sentence aloud with both choices: "On Monday, or monday, we have a test." Circle Monday together. Read each sentence aloud with the class before they choose. Then read the second part of the page together.
1:capitals-names-days-months.stuck: Ask the child, "Is this word a name, a day, or a month? Does it start the sentence?" If yes, it gets a capital letter.

1:characters-setting-events.say: "Read the story at the top of the page. Then write who is in it, where it takes place, and what happens."
1:characters-setting-events.first: Read the title and the story aloud to the class while the children follow with a finger. Then read the first question aloud and ask, "Where in the story does it tell us?" Find the sentence together and finish the first answer together. The children read the story again on their own before they do the rest.
1:characters-setting-events.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its words in the story together. Point to the sentence that has the answer and have the child read it aloud. The answer may be a few words; it does not need to be a long sentence.

1:digraphs.say: "Two letters can make one sound: s-h says sh, c-h says ch, and t-h says th. Say the name of each picture and listen for the letter team."
1:digraphs.first: Write sh, ch, and th on the board and say each sound with the class: sh like a quiet library, ch like a train, th with the tongue between the teeth. Name the pictures together (they are below). Do the first one together.
1:digraphs.stuck: Say the word slowly and stop at the letter team: "mu-sh-room." Then say sh, ch, and th and ask which one it sounds like.

G1-380.say: "Two letters can make one sound: sh, ch, and th. Say the name of each picture. Circle the letter team you hear in it."

G1-392.say: "Each picture word is missing its letter team: sh, ch, or th. Say the word and write the missing letter team in the dashed space."

G1-393.say: "Read each word. Its letter team is marked. Draw a line from the word to the picture it names."
G1-393.first: Write sh, ch, and th on the board and say each sound with the class. Read the first word together, sound by sound, and find its picture. Tell the children to read the letter team as one sound.
G1-393.stuck: Cover the word with a finger and uncover it a part at a time: "ben… ch… bench." Then find the picture together.

G1-588.say: "First read each word and draw a line to its picture; two words have no picture. Then read the words in the second part and write each one under sh or ch."
G1-588.first: Write sh and ch on the board and say each sound with the class. Read the words of the first part aloud together: hip, shelf, chick, chips, ship, kick. Find the first picture together and draw its line. For the second part, read the first word together and ask, "sh or ch?"
G1-588.stuck: Read the word for the child, slowly, and stop at the letter team. Then ask which letter team makes that sound.

digraphs-g1380.first: Write sh, ch, and th on the board and say each sound with the class. Name the pictures together: mushroom, shrimp, chair, chocolate, jellyfish, thumb, bench, feather. Do the first one together: "mushroom: sh." Circle sh. For your own reference: sh: mushroom, shrimp, jellyfish; ch: chair, chocolate, bench; th: thumb, feather.

digraphs-g1392.first: Write sh, ch, and th on the board and say each sound with the class. Name the pictures together: bench, thermometer, chocolate, thumb, shoe, chair, jellyfish, wreath. Do the first one together: "ben…ch." Write ch in the dashed space. For your own reference: ch, th, ch, th, sh, ch, sh, th.

1:doubles-halves.say: "A double is a number added to itself, like 4 + 4. A half is one of two equal parts. Some cards ask for the double, others for the half. Write each answer in the box."
1:doubles-halves.first: Hold up 4 fingers on each hand: "4 and 4 is 8. Eight is the double of four." Then hold up 8 fingers and split them into two equal parts: "Half of 8 is 4." Read the word on the first card, double or half, and do it together.
1:doubles-halves.stuck: For a double, have the child count the pictures and then count them again on from the first number. For a half, have the child share the pictures in two groups, one for you and one for the child, until none are left.

G1-288.say: "Every card cuts a group in half: two equal parts. Write the two equal parts."

1:fact-families.say: "The three numbers on the roof are a family. They make four facts: two adding and two taking away. Use the three numbers to finish all four facts in each house."
1:fact-families.first: Draw a house on the board with 3, 7, and 10 on the roof. Write the four facts together: 3 + 7 = 10, 7 + 3 = 10, 10 − 3 = 7, 10 − 7 = 3. Point out that the biggest number is the whole: it comes after the equals sign when we add and first when we take away.
1:fact-families.stuck: Have the child find the biggest number on the roof and circle it: that is the whole. The other two are the parts. Adding the parts makes the whole; taking a part away from the whole leaves the other part.

1:family-generations.say: "In each row there are family words. Write 1, 2, and 3 to put them in order, from the oldest generation to the youngest."
1:family-generations.first: Talk about a family: grandparents are the oldest generation, then parents, aunts, and uncles, then children like brothers, sisters, and cousins. Read the first row aloud together and ask, "Who is the oldest?" Write 1 under that word, then 2 and 3.
1:family-generations.stuck: Ask the child about each word: "Is that a grandparent, a parent, or a child?" Grandparents get 1, parents 2, children 3. Every family is different; this page is about the words.

G1-386.say: "Read each clue. It tells you who someone is in the family. Write each name in the right name box on the family tree."
G1-386.first: Read the names on the tree and the first clue aloud. Find the child the clues are about on the tree. Ask, "If Leo is Jack's brother, where does he go on the tree?" Write Leo in that box together.
G1-386.stuck: Read the clue with the child and point to Jack on the tree. Ask, "Is a brother next to Jack, above him, or two rows up?" Brothers and sisters are next to him, parents above, grandparents at the top.

1:food-groups.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are boxes: Fruits, Vegetables, Grains, and Protein. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
1:food-groups.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Is this a fruit, a vegetable, a grain like bread or pasta, or a protein like eggs, meat, or fish?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. If a food fits two groups, either box is right when the child can say why.
1:food-groups.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? What is it like?" Then let the child choose the box.

science-sort-g1207-2.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Is this a fruit, a vegetable, a grain like bread or pasta, or a protein like eggs, meat, or fish?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. A tomato can be called a fruit or a vegetable; either box is right for it.

1:habitats-needs.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are boxes: Land, Water, and Air. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
1:habitats-needs.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Where does this animal spend most of its time: on land, in the water, or in the air?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. An animal that flies lives on land too, so Air and Land are both right for it when the child can say why.
1:habitats-needs.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? What is it like?" Then let the child choose the box.

G1-206.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are boxes: Plant Eaters and Meat Eaters. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
G1-206.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "What does this animal eat: plants or other animals?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box.
G1-206.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? What is it like?" Then let the child choose the box.

science-sort-g1202.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "Where does this animal spend most of its time: on land, in the water, or in the air?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. An animal that flies lives on land too, so Air and Land are both right for it, and a crab lives in the water and on land, so Water and Land are both right for it, when the child can say why.

1:info-text-key-details.say: "Read the story at the top of the page. Then write the answer to each question by finishing the sentence."
1:info-text-key-details.first: Read the title and the story aloud to the class while the children follow with a finger. Then read the first question aloud and ask, "Where in the story does it tell us?" Find the sentence together and finish the first answer together. The children read the story again on their own before they do the rest.
1:info-text-key-details.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its words in the story together. Point to the sentence that has the answer and have the child read it aloud. The answer may be a few words; it does not need to be a long sentence.

1:joining-words.say: "A joining word puts two sentences together. And adds one more thing. But tells something you did not expect. So tells what happened because of it. Circle the joining word that fits best in each sentence."
1:joining-words.first: Read the box with the three joining words aloud. Read the first sentence aloud three times, once with each joining word, and ask which one makes the most sense. Circle it. For the last part, read the two sentences together and join them on the lines.
1:joining-words.stuck: Read the sentence with each joining word for the child and ask, "Which one sounds right?" For but, ask, "Is the second part a surprise?"

1:long-or-short-vowel.say: "Say each word. Listen to the colored vowel. Does it say its name, like the a in rake? That is a long vowel: circle the line. Does it make its short sound, like the a in bag? Circle the curve."
1:long-or-short-vowel.first: Write rake and bag on the board and say both: "rake, a says its name: long. bag, a says /a/: short." Read the words on the page aloud together. Do the first one together and circle the line or the curve.
1:long-or-short-vowel.stuck: Say the word slowly and hold the vowel. Then say the letter's name: if the word says the name, it is long.

phonological-awareness-g1495.stuck: Say the word slowly and hold the vowel. Then say the letter's name: if the word says the name, it is long. For your own reference: long: rake, nose, stove, slide; short: chick, bag, fish, nest.

phonological-awareness-g1495-2.stuck: Say the word slowly and hold the vowel. Then say the letter's name: if the word says the name, it is long. For your own reference: long: tape, stove, globe, beet; short: shrimp, nest, leg, sled.

phonological-awareness-g1495-3.stuck: Say the word slowly and hold the vowel. Then say the letter's name: if the word says the name, it is long. For your own reference: long: flute, goat, cube, face; short: rock, sack, hen, shrimp.

1:main-topic-key-details.say: "Read the story at the top of the page. Then write what the whole text is about, the main topic, and two key details: facts the text tells about it."
1:main-topic-key-details.first: Read the title and the story aloud to the class while the children follow with a finger. Then read the first question aloud and ask, "Where in the story does it tell us?" Find the sentence together and finish the first answer together. The children read the story again on their own before they do the rest.
1:main-topic-key-details.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its words in the story together. Point to the sentence that has the answer and have the child read it aloud. The answer may be a few words; it does not need to be a long sentence.

1:map-key.say: "Start at the flag on the grid. Follow the steps, one at a time: each step says which way to move and how many squares. Circle the picture where you land."
1:map-key.first: Put your finger on the flag and read the first step aloud: "Move 1 square right." Move the finger together and stop. Read the next step and move again. Tell the children to count the squares, not the lines, and to keep the finger on the page until the last step.
1:map-key.stuck: Have the child say each step aloud and point with a finger. Check right and left: "Which hand is your right hand? Move that way."

G1-379.say: "The map key shows little pictures and what they stand for. Find each thing from the key on the map, and write how many there are in its box."
G1-379.first: Read the map key aloud together. Find the first thing of the key on the map together and count it; write the number in its box. Tell the children to cross off each one they count so they do not count it twice.
G1-379.stuck: Have the child look at one picture of the key and find all of them on the map, one at a time.

G2-505.say: "Follow the arrows from the flag: each arrow is one step. One arrow is wrong: the path does not end on the star. Find the wrong arrow and fix it."
G2-505.first: Do the first puzzle on the board: put a finger on the flag and move one square for each arrow, saying "up, right, right." See where you land. Then find the arrow that takes the path the wrong way and cross it out.
G2-505.stuck: Have the child move a finger one square per arrow and stop when the path goes off course: that arrow is the wrong one.

1:measure-length-units.say: "Each picture sits on a row of squares. Count the squares from one end of the picture to the other, and write the length."
1:measure-length-units.first: Do the first one together: put a finger on the square under the start of the picture and count each square to the end. Write the number in the box. Tell the children to count only the squares under the picture.
1:measure-length-units.stuck: Have the child make a small mark in each square while counting it.

1:mental-math-to-100.say: "Solve each problem in your head. Think of the tens and the ones. Write the answer in the box."
1:mental-math-to-100.first: Write 36 + 6 on the board. Say, "36 is 3 tens and 6 ones. 6 and 6 make 12, so we get one more ten: 42." Do one taking away ten: 46 − 10 = 36: "only the tens change." Then the children work on their own.
1:mental-math-to-100.stuck: Have the child say the tens and the ones of the first number. For adding or taking away tens, only the tens digit changes; for ones, count on or back from the number.

G1-558.say: "Add or take away tens in your head. Only the tens change. Write the answer in the box."
G1-558.first: Write 34 − 10 on the board and count back by ten together: "34, 24." Ask, "What changed? The tens. The ones stayed 4." Do 56 − 30 together: three tens back: 46, 36, 26.

1:missing-number-equations.say: "In each problem one number is missing. Work out the missing number in your head and write it in the box."
1:missing-number-equations.first: Write 6 + __ = 10 on the board. Ask, "Six and how many more make ten?" Count on from 6 with fingers to 10: four. Write 4. Then do one with take away: 8 − __ = 5.
1:missing-number-equations.stuck: Have the child say the problem aloud with a hum for the box. Count on or back with fingers from the first number to the answer, and count the fingers.

1:number-line-placement.say: "Each arrow points to a mark on the number line. Count on from the number before it and write the number the arrow points to."
1:number-line-placement.first: Draw the first number line on the board. Count the marks with the class from 0, one by one, up to the arrow. Write that number. Tell the children that not every mark has its number written; they count the marks between.
1:number-line-placement.stuck: Have the child find the last printed number before the arrow, put a finger on it, and count each mark up to the arrow.

1:number-words.say: "Each number has a word that we read and write. Read the number and circle the word that matches it."
1:number-words.first: Write 1 to 20 on the board and the words for a few of them. Do the first one together: read the number, read the three words, and circle the matching one.
1:number-words.stuck: Have the child say the number aloud and listen to its first sound; find the word that starts with that letter. Read the words with the child.

G1-227.say: "Find the word for each number in the word bank at the top. Write it on the line."
G1-227.first: Read the words in the word bank aloud together. Do the first one together: read the number, find its word in the bank, and copy it letter by letter.

1:odd-even-pairs.say: "Even numbers can be shared in pairs with none left over. Odd numbers always have one left over. Write each number in the house where it belongs: the odd house or the even house."
1:odd-even-pairs.first: Count by twos together: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10: these are even. Write them on the board. The numbers in between, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, are odd. Tell the children that a number ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 is even. Do the first number together.
1:odd-even-pairs.stuck: Have the child look at the last digit of the number and check it against the list of even numbers on the board. For a small number, draw dots in pairs.

1:ordinal-numbers.say: "Each row of pictures starts at a flag. Find the small picture in the row and write which place it stands in, counting from the flag: first, second, third, and so on."
1:ordinal-numbers.first: Write 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th on the board and read them. Do the first one together: start at the flag, touch each picture and count: "first, second, third." Stop at the small picture and write its place.
1:ordinal-numbers.stuck: Have the child put a finger next to the flag and move to the right one picture at a time, saying the places aloud.

1:retell-and-lesson.say: "Read the story at the top of the page. Then write what happens at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, using the word bank. Then circle the lesson of the story."
1:retell-and-lesson.first: Read the title and the story aloud to the class while the children follow with a finger. Then read the first question aloud and ask, "Where in the story does it tell us?" Find the sentence together and finish the first answer together. The children read the story again on their own before they do the rest.
1:retell-and-lesson.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its words in the story together. Point to the sentence that has the answer and have the child read it aloud. The answer may be a few words; it does not need to be a long sentence.

1:shades-of-meaning.say: "Each row has three words that mean almost the same thing, but some are stronger. Write 1 for the weakest word, 2 for the middle one, and 3 for the strongest."
1:shades-of-meaning.first: Act out the first row: tap the desk softly, knock, then bang. Ask which is the weakest and which is the strongest. Write 1, 2, 3 together. Read every row aloud with the class.
1:shades-of-meaning.stuck: Act the words out with the child or say them with your voice, from a little to a lot.

1:shape-attributes.say: "Look at each shape. Count its sides and corners. Write its name on the line, using the names in the box."
1:shape-attributes.first: Draw a circle, a triangle, a square, and a rectangle on the board and read their names in the box. Do the first shape together: count the sides and choose the name.
1:shape-attributes.stuck: Have the child count the sides with a finger: 3 sides is a triangle; 4 equal sides is a square; 4 sides, two long and two short, is a rectangle; no sides is a circle.

1:sink-float.say: "At the top of the page there are pictures. At the bottom there are boxes: Float and Sink. Draw a line from each picture to the box where it belongs."
1:sink-float.first: Read the words on the boxes aloud and point to each box. Name every picture together, so that everyone knows what it shows. Do the first picture together: ask, "If we put this in water, would it float on top or sink to the bottom?" Draw the line from the dot under the picture to its box. This page asks what the children think; a child who can say why has done the page well.
1:sink-float.stuck: Point to one picture at a time and ask the question of the page about it. If the child is not sure, ask about something the child knows: "Have you ever seen one? What is it like?" Then let the child choose the box.

1:story-key-details.say: "Read the story at the top of the page. Then finish the answer to each question."
1:story-key-details.first: Read the title and the story aloud to the class while the children follow with a finger. Then read the first question aloud and ask, "Where in the story does it tell us?" Find the sentence together and finish the first answer together. The children read the story again on their own before they do the rest.
1:story-key-details.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its words in the story together. Point to the sentence that has the answer and have the child read it aloud. The answer may be a few words; it does not need to be a long sentence.

1:synonyms.say: "Synonyms are words that mean the same thing, like big and large. Under each picture there are words. Circle the two words that mean the same and tell about the picture."
1:synonyms.first: Write big and large on the board: "They mean the same." Look at the first picture together and read its words aloud. Ask, "Which two mean the same and fit the picture?" Circle them.
1:synonyms.stuck: Read the words with the child and ask, "Which word could you put in place of this one?"

1:true-false-equations.say: "Is each number sentence true? If both sides are the same amount, it is true: circle the check mark. If not, it is false: circle the X."
1:true-false-equations.first: Write 10 − 2 = 8 on the board and ask, "Is ten take away two eight? Yes: true." Write 9 = 5 + 6 and ask, "Is five and six nine? No: false." Remind the children that the equals sign means "the same as" and can be on either side.
1:true-false-equations.stuck: Have the child work out the side with the plus or minus sign and then compare it with the number on the other side.

1:true-story-plan-and-draft.say: "Time words like first, next, and last tell the order of a story. First read the little story and circle its time words. Then plan your own true story in the boxes."
1:true-story-plan-and-draft.first: Read the story on the page aloud and circle the time words together: first, then, last. Do the numbering part together. For the plan, let a few children say an idea: a rainy day, something new they learned. Each child draws and writes a few words in each box: First, Next, Last, and how they felt.
1:true-story-plan-and-draft.stuck: Ask the child, "What did you do first? And then?" Write one word for the child to copy, or let the child draw and label.

1:verb-tense.say: "A verb tells when something happens: yesterday I walked, today I walk, tomorrow I will walk. Write the missing verbs. Then circle the verb that fits the time word in each sentence."
1:verb-tense.first: Write walked, walk, will walk under Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow on the board. Do the first row on the page together. For the second part, read the first sentence aloud and look for the time word: yesterday, today, or tomorrow.
1:verb-tense.stuck: Ask, "Did it happen already, is it happening now, or will it happen later?" Already: add -ed. Later: will.

K:grid-copy.say: "Look at the picture on the small grid. Color the same squares on the empty grid so the picture appears again."
K:grid-copy.first: Point to the letters across the top and the numbers down the side. Find one colored square together, say its letter and number, and color the same square on the empty grid. Tell the children to do one row at a time.
K:grid-copy.stuck: Have the child put one finger on a colored square and another on the same row and column of the empty grid.

K-502.say: "Look at the picture on the small grid. Color the same squares on the big grid, where every square is twice as big."
K-502.first: Find the top-left colored square on the small grid together and count which row and which column it is in. Find the same row and column on the big grid and color that square. Tell the children to do one row at a time.

K-299.say: "Use the letter and number of each square to copy the picture onto the empty grid."

K-300.say: "A bigger grid: find each square by its letter and number, and copy the picture onto the empty grid."

1:question-words.say: "Read each answer. Look at the highlighted words. Which question asks for them: who, what, where, when, or how many? Write that question word in the box."
1:question-words.first: Read the question words in the bank aloud. Read the first answer and its question aloud and look at the highlighted words. Ask, "Which question word asks for these words?" Write it in the box together. Do the rest of the page by reading each answer aloud with the class.
1:question-words.stuck: Ask the child: "Is the highlighted part a person? Then who. A thing? What. A place? Where. A time? When. A number? How many."

1:bar-model.say: "Each bar shows a whole and its two parts. One number is missing. Write the missing number in the box."
1:bar-model.first: Draw a bar on the board split into two parts, with 60 on top as the whole and 20 in one part. Ask, "What goes with 20 to make 60?" Count on by tens together: 30, 40, 50, 60: forty. Write it in the empty part. Tell the children to check whether the missing number is a part or the whole.
1:bar-model.stuck: Ask, "Is the whole missing? Then add the two parts. Is a part missing? Then take the other part away from the whole."

1:check-answers.say: "Someone has already solved these problems, but some answers are wrong. Check each one. If it is wrong, put an X in the small box and write the right answer in the big box. If it is right, leave both boxes empty."
1:check-answers.first: Do the first problem on the board together: solve it yourself and compare with the answer that is printed. "Is it the same? Then leave both boxes empty. If not, an X and the right answer." Tell the children to solve each problem first and only then look at the printed answer.
1:check-answers.stuck: Have the child cover the printed answer, solve the problem with fingers or a drawing, and then uncover the answer and compare.

2:adjective-or-adverb.say: "An adjective tells about a noun: a brave dog. An adverb tells how something is done: the dog ran bravely. Many adverbs end in -ly. Circle the word that fits each sentence, then draw an arrow to the word it tells about."
2:adjective-or-adverb.first: Write "a quick fox" and "the fox ran quickly" on the board. Ask which word tells about the fox and which tells how it ran. Read the first sentence on the page aloud with both choices and circle the one that fits together. Read the rule box about words ending in y aloud.
2:adjective-or-adverb.stuck: Ask, "Does the word tell about a thing, or about how someone does something?" A thing gets the adjective; how someone does something gets the -ly word.

2:bossy-r-ar-or.say: "When r comes after a vowel, it bosses the vowel and changes its sound. A-r says ar, like in park. O-r says or, like in storm. Read each word and write it under ar or or."
2:bossy-r-ar-or.first: Write park and storm on the board and read them with the class. Read the first word on the page aloud together, listen for ar or or, and write it under its heading. Then read the second part of the page aloud together.
2:bossy-r-ar-or.stuck: Have the child look at the letter before the r: a-r is ar, o-r is or. Read the word together slowly.

2:bundle-ten-ones.say: "Count the blocks in each picture. Ten small cubes make a ten, and ten tens make a hundred. Write the number they show."
