2:bundle-ten-ones.first: Draw a flat (a hundred), two rods, and four small cubes on the board. Count together: "one hundred, one hundred ten, one hundred twenty, and four more: one hundred twenty-four." Tell the children that when there are ten or more cubes of one kind, they bundle ten into the next place. Do the first picture together.
2:bundle-ten-ones.stuck: Have the child count each kind first: hundreds, tens, ones. If there are more than nine ones, circle ten of them: that is one more ten.

2:cardinal-directions.say: "The four directions are north, east, south, and west. On a compass rose, north is at the tip that points up. Write the three missing letters in the empty boxes."
2:cardinal-directions.first: Draw a compass rose on the board: N at the top, S at the bottom, E on the right, W on the left. Say "Never Eat Soggy Waffles" going round from the top. On the page the orange tip points north, and it may not point up: turn the page so the orange tip points up, then fill in the boxes. Do the first rose together.
2:cardinal-directions.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the orange tip and say north, then go around clockwise: east, south, west.

G2-371.say: "Look at the map. Start at the first picture of each question, look the way the word says, and circle the picture you see in that direction."
G2-371.first: Find the compass rose on the map together and say the four directions. Read the first question aloud, put a finger on its first picture, and move the finger the way the word says. Circle the picture you reach. Use the map key to name the pictures.
G2-371.stuck: Have the child point to the direction on the compass rose first, then move a finger the same way across the map.

2:character-challenge.say: "Read the text at the top of the page carefully. Then write the answer to each question."
2:character-challenge.first: Read the title and the first part of the text aloud while the children follow. Then the children read it again on their own. Read the first question aloud together and ask, "Where in the text can we find this?" Find the sentence together and write the first answer together. Ask the class, "What is the character's problem? What does the character do about it?"
2:character-challenge.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the text together. Point to the part that has the answer and have the child read it aloud before writing.

2:continents.say: "The map shows the seven continents, each with a number. Write the name of each continent on its line. The names are in the box."
2:continents.first: Read the seven names in the box aloud together. Point to North America on the map: "This is where the United States is." Find its number together and write North America on that line. The children do the rest, crossing each name out of the box when they use it.
2:continents.stuck: Give clues: "Antarctica is the icy one at the bottom. South America is under North America. Africa is the big one in the middle." Let the child find each one on the map.

2:diagram-and-text.say: "Read the text at the top of the page carefully. Then use the diagram to answer the questions. Questions 1 to 3 ask about the diagram; the others ask about the text."
2:diagram-and-text.first: Read the title and the first part of the text aloud while the children follow. Then the children read it again on their own. Read the first question aloud together and ask, "Where in the text can we find this?" Find the sentence together and write the first answer together. Show the children how to follow the arrows of the diagram from the first picture to the last.
2:diagram-and-text.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the text together. Point to the part that has the answer and have the child read it aloud before writing.

2:draft-an-opinion.say: "Today you write an opinion piece: what you think and why. Circle one question. Write your opinion, give your reasons, and end with a closing sentence."
2:draft-an-opinion.first: Read both questions aloud and let a few children say their opinion and one reason. Write the parts on the board: I think … because … Also … That is why … Each child circles one question and writes.
2:draft-an-opinion.stuck: Have the child tell you the idea aloud first; then say, "Write that." Help with the first words of a sentence, and let the child spell words the way they sound. A short, finished piece is better than a long, unfinished one.

2:er-ir-ur.say: "Er, ir, and ur all say the same sound, like in her, first, and turn. Read each word and write it under er, ir, or ur."
2:er-ir-ur.first: Write her, first, and turn on the board and read them with the class. Read the first word on the page together and look at its letters: which spelling does it use? Write it under that heading. Read the second part of the page aloud together.
2:er-ir-ur.stuck: Point out that the sound is the same, so the child looks at the letters, not the sound: is it e-r, i-r, or u-r?

2:fable-lesson.say: "Read the text at the top of the page carefully. Then write its lesson, the thing a reader learns from it, and what a character does that shows the lesson."
2:fable-lesson.first: Read the title and the first part of the text aloud while the children follow. Then the children read it again on their own. Read the first question aloud together and ask, "Where in the text can we find this?" Find the sentence together and write the first answer together. After reading, ask, "What does the story teach us?"
2:fable-lesson.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the text together. Point to the part that has the answer and have the child read it aloud before writing.

2:fraction-of-a-set.say: "Each row shows a group of pictures and a fraction. Circle that part of the group, and write how many that is."
2:fraction-of-a-set.first: Draw 8 circles on the board. Say, "One half means two equal groups. Half of 8 is 4." Circle 4. For one fourth, make four equal groups and circle one group. Do the first row together.
2:fraction-of-a-set.stuck: Have the child share the pictures into as many equal groups as the bottom number says, one picture at a time. Then circle as many groups as the top number says.

2:friendly-letter.say: "A friendly letter has five parts: the date, the greeting, the body, the closing, and the signature. Write the name of each part on its line, using the word bank."
2:friendly-letter.first: Read the five parts in the word bank aloud and find each one in the letter on the page together: the date at the top, "Dear…" is the greeting, the long middle is the body, "Your friend" is the closing, and the name at the end is the signature. Do the first one together.
2:friendly-letter.stuck: Ask, "Where does a letter start? Who is it to? Who wrote it?" Point to each part as you ask.

2:life-cycles.say: "A butterfly grows in four stages. Write the four stage names from the word bank on the lines under their pictures. Then cross out the name that is not part of a butterfly's life."
2:life-cycles.first: Read the word bank aloud together. Ask, "What does a butterfly start as?" An egg. Find the egg picture and write egg under it together. Talk through the order: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. A tadpole is a baby frog.
2:life-cycles.stuck: Have the child follow the arrows from the egg and name what each picture shows.

G2-366.say: "Look at each stage, like an egg, a tadpole, or a caterpillar. Write its letter in a box under the animal it will grow into. Some boxes stay empty."
G2-366.first: Name the grown-up animals together, then look at the first stage and ask, "What will this become?" Write its letter in a box under that animal.
G2-366.stuck: Ask the child which animal the stage looks a little like, or say what the stage is called: a tadpole becomes a frog, a caterpillar becomes a butterfly.

2:line-plots.say: "A line plot shows how many with X marks above each number. Count the X marks above each number and write how many."
2:line-plots.first: Draw a short number line on the board with a few X marks above the numbers. Count the X marks above one number together and write the count. Do the first question on the page together.
2:line-plots.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the number and count the X marks straight above it, from the bottom up.

2:plan-informative-piece.say: "An informative piece teaches facts. It has a topic sentence that tells what it is about, facts, and a closing sentence. Read the parts at the top, then do each part of the page."
2:plan-informative-piece.first: Read the box with the parts of an informative piece aloud. Do the first task of the page together: find the topic sentence, a fact, or the closing sentence. Then the children go on.
2:plan-informative-piece.stuck: Have the child tell you the idea aloud first; then say, "Write that." Help with the first words of a sentence, and let the child spell words the way they sound. A short, finished piece is better than a long, unfinished one.

2:road-signs.say: "Each road sign has a letter. Some signs tell a rule, and some warn about danger. Write the letter of each sign in the boxes of its group."
2:road-signs.first: Look at the signs together and say what each one means. Ask about the first sign, "Does it tell drivers what they must do, like stop? Or does it warn them about something ahead?" Write its letter in the right group.
2:road-signs.stuck: Talk through the shape: many warning signs are yellow diamonds, many rule signs are white rectangles or red, like STOP.

G2-361.say: "Read each sentence. Circle the one road sign that fits it."
G2-361.first: Read the first sentence aloud and look at the three signs next to it. Ask, "Which sign tells drivers about this?" Circle it together. Read each sentence aloud for children who need it.
G2-361.stuck: Read the sentence again and name the three signs; ask which one would help in that place.

2:short-or-long-vowel.say: "A short vowel says its sound: hop. A long vowel says its name: hope. Read each word and write it under short vowel or long vowel."
2:short-or-long-vowel.first: Write hop and hope on the board and read them. Point out the e at the end and the two vowels together that often make a long sound, like ee and ay. Read the first word on the page together and decide.
2:short-or-long-vowel.stuck: Say the word slowly and hold the vowel. Then say the letter's name: if the word says the name, it is long.

2:steps-in-order.say: "Read the text at the top of the page carefully. Then write the four steps in order. The first word of each step is given."
2:steps-in-order.first: Read the title and the first part of the text aloud while the children follow. Then the children read it again on their own. Read the first question aloud together and ask, "Where in the text can we find this?" Find the sentence together and write the first answer together. Ask the class to look for the words first, then, next, and last in the text.
2:steps-in-order.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the text together. Point to the part that has the answer and have the child read it aloud before writing.

2:subtract-with-blocks.say: "The first number is drawn on the tens-and-ones mat. Are there enough ones to take away? Mark yes or no. If there are not enough, trade one ten for ten ones. Then subtract and write the answer."
2:subtract-with-blocks.first: Do the first problem on the board: draw the tens and ones of the first number. Ask, "Can we take away the ones?" If not, cross out one ten and draw ten more ones. Then cross out the ones and tens to take away and count what is left.
2:subtract-with-blocks.stuck: Have the child compare the ones: "Do we have more ones than we take away?" If not, trade a ten. Count the leftover tens and ones together.

2:suffixes-ful-less-ly.say: "A suffix is a word part at the end. -ful means full of, -less means without, and -ly tells how. Circle the base word in each word and underline the suffix. Then match each word to its meaning."
2:suffixes-ful-less-ly.first: Write playful on the board: circle play, underline -ful. Ask, "What does playful mean? Full of play." Do the same with toothless. Do the first word on the page together.
2:suffixes-ful-less-ly.stuck: Cover the suffix with a finger and read the base word. Then add the suffix and ask what the whole word means.

2:true-story-plan-draft.say: "A true story tells what really happened, in order. Read the parts of a true story at the top, then do each part of the page."
2:true-story-plan-draft.first: Read the box at the top aloud: beginning, middle with time words, and an ending. Do the first task together. For a plan, let a few children say their idea first.
2:true-story-plan-draft.stuck: Have the child tell you the idea aloud first; then say, "Write that." Help with the first words of a sentence, and let the child spell words the way they sound. A short, finished piece is better than a long, unfinished one.

2:two-step-word-problems.say: "Read each story. Write the question if it is missing, then the equation and the answer."
2:two-step-word-problems.first: Read the first story aloud. Ask, "What do we need to find out?" Write the equation on the board together and solve it with tens and ones. Then the children read the other stories on their own.
2:two-step-word-problems.stuck: Read the story with the child and underline the numbers. Ask, "Are things put together, or taken away?" Draw a quick bar to show the parts and the whole.

G2-510.say: "Read each story. In the bar model, write the two numbers you know and a question mark for the number you need. Then solve."
G2-510.first: Read the first story aloud. Ask, "Do we know the start? The change? The end?" Write the two numbers you know in the bar and a question mark where the missing number goes. Solve it together.

G2-511.say: "Each story has two steps. Do the first step, then the second step. Write the numbers in the boxes."
G2-511.first: Read the first story aloud. Ask, "What happens first? What happens next?" Do step a together, then step b with the answer of step a.

2:two-versions-of-a-tale.say: "Two versions of one tale can have different characters and settings. Read both versions. Sort each fact: is it in version 1, version 2, or both?"
2:two-versions-of-a-tale.first: Read the two versions aloud while the children follow. Then read the first fact aloud and ask, "Which version tells this?" Write it in the right place together.
2:two-versions-of-a-tale.stuck: Read the fact with the child and look for it in each version, one at a time.

2:vowel-teams-long-a-e-o.say: "Two vowels together can make one long sound. Ai and ay spell long a, ee and ea spell long e, oa and ow spell long o. Read each word and write it under its vowel sound."
2:vowel-teams-long-a-e-o.first: Write rain, play, feet, eat, boat, and snow on the board and read them. Read the first word on the page together, find its vowel team, and write it under its sound.
2:vowel-teams-long-a-e-o.stuck: Have the child find the two vowels together and say the long sound they make.

2:words-in-real-life.say: "Describing words tell what real things are like: hot soup, a soft blanket. Read each sentence and do what the page asks."
2:words-in-real-life.first: Read the first part of the page aloud with the class and do its first item together. Ask, "What is this thing really like? Which word fits?"
2:words-in-real-life.stuck: Ask the child to think of a real one: "Have you touched one? Is it hard or soft, hot or cold?"

3:answer-with-evidence.say: "Read the text carefully, all the way to the end. Then write each answer. In the box, write the number of the paragraph that proves your answer."
3:answer-with-evidence.first: Read the title and the first paragraph aloud while the children follow; they read the rest on their own. Read the first question aloud and ask, "Which paragraph tells us?" Find it together and write the first answer together. Show the children the small numbers at the start of the paragraphs.
3:answer-with-evidence.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the text. Have the child put a finger on the paragraph that answers it and read it aloud before writing. A short answer in the child's own words is fine.

G3-495.say: "Read the text. Each sentence in a box comes from the text. Write the question that the sentence answers. The first one is started for you."
G3-495.first: Read the text aloud with the class. Read the first sentence in a box and ask, "What question does this answer?" Look at how the first one is started and finish it together. A question ends with a question mark.
G3-495.stuck: Have the child find the sentence in the text and ask, "What would someone ask to get this answer: who, what, where, when, why, or how?"

3:central-message.say: "Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. Then write its central message, the lesson it teaches, and three things in the story that show it."
3:central-message.first: Read the title and the first paragraph aloud while the children follow; they read the rest on their own. Read the first question aloud and ask, "Which paragraph tells us?" Find it together and write the first answer together. After reading, ask, "What does this story teach us?"
3:central-message.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the story. Have the child put a finger on the paragraph that answers it and read it aloud before writing. A short answer in the child's own words is fine.

G3-505.say: "Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. Then retell it: write the four main events in order."
G3-505.first: Read the title and the first paragraph aloud while the children follow; they read the rest on their own. Read the first question aloud and ask, "Which paragraph tells us?" Find it together and write the first answer together. Ask the class, "What happens first? What is the most important thing that happens next?"
G3-505.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the story. Have the child put a finger on the paragraph that answers it and read it aloud before writing. A short answer in the child's own words is fine.

3:events-cause-effect.say: "Read the text carefully, all the way to the end. Then write the four events or steps in order."
3:events-cause-effect.first: Read the title and the first paragraph aloud while the children follow; they read the rest on their own. Read the first question aloud and ask, "Which paragraph tells us?" Find it together and write the first answer together. Look for time words like first, then, and later together.
3:events-cause-effect.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the text. Have the child put a finger on the paragraph that answers it and read it aloud before writing. A short answer in the child's own words is fine.

G3-501.say: "Read the text carefully, all the way to the end. Then write the missing cause or effect. A cause makes something happen; an effect is what happens."
G3-501.first: Read the title and the first paragraph aloud while the children follow; they read the rest on their own. Read the first question aloud and ask, "Which paragraph tells us?" Find it together and write the first answer together. Write "Because it rained, the game was canceled" on the board: the rain is the cause, the canceled game the effect.
G3-501.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the text. Have the child put a finger on the paragraph that answers it and read it aloud before writing. A short answer in the child's own words is fine.

3:main-idea-key-details.say: "Read the text carefully, all the way to the end. Then write the main idea of the whole text and three key details that support it."
3:main-idea-key-details.first: Read the title and the first paragraph aloud while the children follow; they read the rest on their own. Read the first question aloud and ask, "Which paragraph tells us?" Find it together and write the first answer together. Ask, "What is the whole text mostly about?" before the children write.
3:main-idea-key-details.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the text. Have the child put a finger on the paragraph that answers it and read it aloud before writing. A short answer in the child's own words is fine.

G3-497.say: "Read the text carefully, all the way to the end. Then write what each paragraph is mostly about."
G3-497.first: Read the title and the first paragraph aloud while the children follow; they read the rest on their own. Read the first question aloud and ask, "Which paragraph tells us?" Find it together and write the first answer together. Do the first paragraph together: read it and say in a few words what it is mostly about.
G3-497.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the text. Have the child put a finger on the paragraph that answers it and read it aloud before writing. A short answer in the child's own words is fine.

3:story-evidence.say: "Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. Then write each answer. In the box, write the number of the paragraph that proves your answer."
3:story-evidence.first: Read the title and the first paragraph aloud while the children follow; they read the rest on their own. Read the first question aloud and ask, "Which paragraph tells us?" Find it together and write the first answer together. Show the children the small numbers at the start of the paragraphs.
3:story-evidence.stuck: Read the question with the child and look for its key words in the story. Have the child put a finger on the paragraph that answers it and read it aloud before writing. A short answer in the child's own words is fine.

G3-503.say: "Read the story. Each sentence in a box comes from the story. Write the question that the sentence answers. The first one is started for you."
G3-503.first: Read the story aloud with the class. Read the first sentence in a box and ask, "What question does this answer?" Look at how the first one is started and finish it together.
G3-503.stuck: Have the child find the sentence in the story and ask, "What would someone ask to get this answer: who, what, where, when, why, or how?"

3:closed-open-syllables.say: "A closed syllable ends with a consonant, and its vowel is short: rab in rabbit. An open syllable ends with a vowel, and the vowel says its name: ro in robot. Read each word, draw a line between its syllables, and write C or O for each one."
3:closed-open-syllables.first: Read the box at the top aloud. Write robot and rabbit on the board, split them together (ro|bot, rab|bit), and mark each part C or O. Read the first word on the page together and do it.
3:closed-open-syllables.stuck: Have the child look at the letters between the two vowels. Two consonants: split between them. One consonant: split after the first vowel and say it long; if that is not a word, split after the consonant and say it short. A part that ends with a vowel is open, a part that ends with a consonant is closed.

G3-513.say: "A closed syllable ends with a consonant, and its vowel is short: rab in rabbit. An open syllable ends with a vowel, and the vowel says its name: ro in robot. Read each word and write it under its heading, closed or open first syllable, with a line between its syllables. Then answer each sentence with yes or no."
G3-513.first: Read the two headings aloud. Write tiger and napkin on the board and split them together: ti|ger has an open first syllable with a long i, nap|kin a closed one with a short a. Read the first word on the page together and write it under its heading.

3:context-clues.say: "When you do not know a word, the words around it can help. The box at the top shows four kinds of clues: a definition, a synonym, an antonym, and an example. Read each sentence and do what the page asks."
3:context-clues.first: Read the box at the top aloud with an example of each kind. Read the first sentence on the page aloud and find the clue together: "Which words help us know what it means?"
3:context-clues.stuck: Read the sentence with the child and cover the new word. Ask, "What word could go here?" Then find the words that helped.

3:parts-of-speech.say: "Every word has a job. A noun names something, a pronoun takes its place, a verb shows an action or being, an adjective tells about a noun, and an adverb tells how. Label each word by its job."
3:parts-of-speech.first: Read the box with the letters for each job aloud. Read the first sentence on the page aloud and label its first word together: "What job does this word do here?"
3:parts-of-speech.stuck: Ask the questions one by one: "Is it a thing? Does it replace a name? Is it something you do? Does it describe a thing? Does it tell how?"

G3-531.say: "Every word has a job. A noun names something, a pronoun takes its place, a verb shows an action or being, an adjective tells about a noun, and an adverb tells how, when, or how often. Write each word in the column of its job and cross it out. Then write two more words of your own for each job."

3:plural-nouns.say: "A plural noun names more than one. Its spelling follows a rule: add -s; add -es after s, x, z, ch, or sh; change y to i and add -es; some words change completely. Read the rules at the top and do each part of the page."
3:plural-nouns.first: Read the rule box aloud and write one example of each rule on the board: cats, boxes, babies, leaves. Do the first item on the page together and say which rule it follows.
3:plural-nouns.stuck: Have the child look at the last letter or letters of the word and find the matching rule in the box.

3:past-tense-verbs.say: "Regular verbs add -ed in the past: walk, walked. Irregular verbs change: go, went. Read the rules at the top and do each part of the page."
3:past-tense-verbs.first: Read the rule box aloud with an example of each rule. Do the first item on the page together and say which rule it follows.
3:past-tense-verbs.stuck: Ask the child to say the verb in a sentence with "yesterday": "Yesterday I…" The word they say is often the past tense; then check its spelling with the rules.

G3-535.say: "This little story is told in the present. Rewrite it in the past tense: change every numbered verb to its yesterday form."
G3-535.first: Read the story aloud. Do the first numbered verb together: "make… yesterday we made." Write it on the line. Remind the children that some verbs just add -ed and some change.
G3-535.stuck: Have the child read the sentence with "yesterday" at the start and say the verb that sounds right.

3:possessive-nouns.say: "An apostrophe shows who owns something. One owner: add apostrophe s, the bee's hive. More than one owner that ends in s: add the apostrophe after the s, the bees' hives. Read the box and do each part of the page."
3:possessive-nouns.first: Read the box at the top aloud. Write the bee's hive and the bees' hives on the board and ask how many bees there are in each. Do the first item together: "How many owners?"
3:possessive-nouns.stuck: Ask the child, "Is there one owner or more than one?" Then point to the matching rule in the box.

3:suffixes-able-ment-ness-ful-less.say: "A suffix at the end changes a word: kind and -ness make kindness. Read each word, circle the base word, and underline the suffix. Then do the rest of the page."
3:suffixes-able-ment-ness-ful-less.first: Write kindness on the board: circle kind, underline -ness. Ask what it means: being kind. Do the first word on the page together.
3:suffixes-able-ment-ness-ful-less.stuck: Cover the suffix with a finger and read the base word. Then read the whole word and ask what it means.

3:dialogue-and-description.say: "Quotation marks go around the exact words someone says. A comma or an end mark goes inside the closing quotation mark: “We won,” said Kim. Read the box and do each part of the page."
3:dialogue-and-description.first: Read the box at the top aloud. Write a line of dialogue on the board and point to each mark. Do the first item on the page together.
3:dialogue-and-description.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the words the person says: they go inside the quotation marks, and the comma or end mark goes in with them.

3:joining-words.say: "A joining word shows how two ideas go together. And adds another idea, because tells why, but shows a difference, and so tells the result. Join the sentences with a word from the box."
3:joining-words.first: Read the box aloud. Read the first two sentences aloud and try each joining word between them. Ask which one makes sense and write the joined sentence together.
3:joining-words.stuck: Read the two sentences with each joining word and ask, "Which one tells how they go together?"

3:linking-words.say: "Linking words join an opinion to its reasons. Because and since tell why. Therefore tells what happens as a result. For example gives an example. Circle the linking word that fits each sentence."
3:linking-words.first: Read the box at the top aloud. Read the first sentence aloud with each linking word and circle the one that fits together.
3:linking-words.stuck: Ask, "Does the second part give a reason, a result, or an example?" Then find the word for it in the box.

G3-551.say: "Write your opinion piece. Choose one question, state your opinion, give reasons, and join them with linking words. End with a closing sentence."
G3-551.first: Read the questions aloud and let a few children say an opinion and a reason. Write a frame on the board: In my opinion … because … Also, … For example, … That is why … Each child circles one question and writes.
G3-551.stuck: Have the child tell you the idea aloud first; then say, "Write that." Help with the first words of a sentence, and let the child spell words as well as they can. A short, finished piece is better than a long, unfinished one.

3:opinion-and-reasons.say: "An opinion piece tells what the writer thinks and gives reasons for it. A fact can be checked and proved true. Read the box at the top and do each part of the page."
3:opinion-and-reasons.first: Read the box at the top aloud. Write "Dogs are the best pets" and "Dogs have four legs" on the board and ask which is an opinion and which is a fact. Do the first item on the page together.
3:opinion-and-reasons.stuck: Ask, "Can everyone agree, and can we check it? Then it is a fact. Could people disagree? Then it is an opinion."

G3-549.say: "Plan your opinion piece before you write: choose a question, write your opinion, and give reasons that tell why."
G3-549.first: Read the questions aloud and let a few children say their opinion and one reason. Each child circles a question and fills in the plan.
G3-549.stuck: Have the child tell you the idea aloud first; then say, "Write that." Help with the first words of a sentence, and let the child spell words as well as they can. A short, finished piece is better than a long, unfinished one.

3:plan-a-story.say: "Every story has characters, a setting, a problem, and a narrator who tells it. Read the box at the top and do each part of the page."
3:plan-a-story.first: Read the box at the top aloud and name the parts in a story the class knows. Do the first item on the page together.
3:plan-a-story.stuck: Ask the child, "Who is in the story? Where is it? What goes wrong? Who tells it?"

G3-565.say: "Plan your story: choose a story idea, then plan the beginning, the middle, and the end."
G3-565.first: Read the story ideas aloud and let a few children say what could happen. Each child circles an idea and fills in the plan: who and where at the beginning, the problem in the middle, how it is solved at the end.
G3-565.stuck: Have the child tell you the idea aloud first; then say, "Write that." Help with the first words of a sentence, and let the child spell words as well as they can. A short, finished piece is better than a long, unfinished one.

3:time-words-in-stories.say: "Time words like first, later that day, and finally tell when things happen in a story. Read the box at the top and do each part of the page."
3:time-words-in-stories.first: Read the box of time words aloud. Do the first item on the page together and say where the time word goes.
3:time-words-in-stories.stuck: Ask the child, "Does this happen at the start, in the middle, or at the end?" Then pick a time word from that part of the box.

G3-569.say: "Write a short story with time words, so a reader can follow the events in order. Read the example first."
G3-569.first: Read the example story aloud and point to its time words. Let a few children say a story idea. Each child writes a story with at least three time words.
G3-569.stuck: Have the child tell you the idea aloud first; then say, "Write that." Help with the first words of a sentence, and let the child spell words as well as they can. A short, finished piece is better than a long, unfinished one.

3:compare-fractions.say: "Each row has two fraction bars. Look at both bars. Circle the bigger fraction."
3:compare-fractions.first: Draw two bars of the same length on the board, one cut into halves and one into fourths. Shade one half and one fourth and ask which is bigger. Do the first row on the page together: compare how much of each bar is shaded.
3:compare-fractions.stuck: Have the child compare the shaded parts of the two bars side by side. When the bars are the same size, the longer shaded part is the bigger fraction.

3:division-sharing.say: "Share the pile equally into the bins. Write how many each bin gets. That is division: 12 ÷ 3 means 12 shared into 3 equal groups."
3:division-sharing.first: Draw 12 dots and 3 circles on the board. Share the dots one at a time into the circles and count each circle: 4. Write 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Do the first problem on the page together.
3:division-sharing.stuck: Have the child share the pictures one by one, crossing each off, until none is left. Then count one bin.

3:equivalent-fractions.say: "Some fractions look different but show the same amount, like one half and two fourths. Draw a line from each picture to the fraction that shows the same amount."
3:equivalent-fractions.first: Draw two bars of the same length: one with one half shaded, one with two fourths shaded. Show that the shaded parts are the same length. Do the first picture on the page together: count the parts and the shaded parts.
3:equivalent-fractions.stuck: Have the child count the equal parts (the bottom number) and the shaded parts (the top number) of the picture, then find the fraction that matches.

3:mult-equal-groups.say: "Count the equal groups and how many are in each group. Finish the multiplication: the number of groups times the number in each group."
3:mult-equal-groups.first: Draw 3 groups of 4 dots on the board. Count the groups and the dots in one group: 3 groups of 4 is 3 × 4 = 12. Do the first one on the page together.
3:mult-equal-groups.stuck: Have the child count by the number in each group: 4, 8, 12. The number of groups is how many times they count.

3:right-angles.say: "A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a sheet of paper. Circle every right angle on the page."
3:right-angles.first: Hold up a sheet of paper and show its square corner. Show the children how to check a corner on the page with the corner of a sheet of paper or an index card. Find one right angle together and circle it.
3:right-angles.stuck: Give the child a scrap of paper and have them hold its corner in each angle: if it fits exactly, it is a right angle.

3:scaled-graphs.say: "Careful: on this graph each line of the scale counts by five, not by one. Read the value of each bar and write it."
3:scaled-graphs.first: Point to the scale on the side and count it together: 0, 5, 10, 15. Read the first bar together: slide a finger from its top across to the scale. If it stops between two lines, it is halfway between them.
3:scaled-graphs.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the top of the bar and move it straight across to the scale, then count by fives from zero up to that line.

3:time-to-minute.say: "Read each clock to the minute. The short hand shows the hour. Count the minutes by fives, then by ones. Circle the time that matches."
3:time-to-minute.first: Draw a clock on the board with the long hand two marks after the 4. Count by fives to the 4 (20) and then by ones (21, 22): 22 minutes. Do the first clock on the page together.
3:time-to-minute.stuck: Have the child count by fives to the number before the long hand, then count each small mark by ones.

2:mass-grams.say: "Read each measuring cup and balance scale. Write the amount with its unit: grams for the scale, milliliters for the cup."
2:mass-grams.first: Point to the numbers on the first cup or scale and count the marks between them together. Read where the line or the pointer is and write the amount with its unit.
2:mass-grams.stuck: Have the child find the printed number just below the line and count the marks up to it.

2:moon-phases.say: "Look at each moon. Write its name on the lines: new moon, first quarter, full moon, or last quarter. Use each word in the word bank twice."
2:moon-phases.first: Read the word bank aloud. Draw a full moon (all bright) and a new moon (dark) on the board. A quarter moon shows half of the circle bright. Do the first moon on the page together.
2:moon-phases.stuck: Ask the child, "Is it all bright, all dark, or half bright?" A half-bright moon is a quarter: first quarter when the right side is bright, last quarter when the left side is.

2:day-and-night.say: "Look where the Sun is. The side of Earth that faces the Sun has day; the other side has night. At each numbered pin, is it day or night? Circle the word in the table."
2:day-and-night.first: Point from the Sun on the page to Earth and show the side that faces it. Do the first pin together: "Does it face the Sun?" Circle day or night.
2:day-and-night.stuck: Have the child trace a line from the Sun to the pin: if Earth is in the way, it is night there.

2:sink-float.say: "The same clay can sink or float: a ball of clay sinks, a clay boat floats. Color the ring where each clay shape ends up, circle the thing that floats, then draw your own clay boat."
2:sink-float.first: Talk about the pictures: a ball and a flat boat made of the same clay. Ask, "Which one floats? Why?" Do the first part together.
2:sink-float.stuck: Ask the child, "Is it flat and wide like a boat, or a tight ball?"

G2-383.say: "Read each sentence about things that sink and float, and circle true or false."
G2-383.first: Name the pictures at the top together. Read the first sentence aloud and ask, "Is that true?" Talk about it, then circle.
G2-383.stuck: Ask the child what happens to that thing in a bathtub or a pool.

3:continents-oceans.say: "The map shows the continents and the oceans, each with a number. Find each one on the map and write its number in the box next to its name."
3:continents-oceans.first: Read the names aloud together. Point to North America: "This is where the United States is." Find its number and write it next to North America together. The oceans are the big blue areas.
3:continents-oceans.stuck: Give clues: "The Pacific is the biggest ocean, on the left and right. Antarctica is the icy land at the bottom." Let the child find each one.

3:elapsed-duration.say: "Each row shows a start clock and an end clock. Read both and write how much time passed. The word next to the box tells you to answer in hours or in minutes."
3:elapsed-duration.first: Read the two clocks of the first row together and write both times on the board. Count on from the start time to the end time: by hours when the box says hours, by fives when it says minutes. Write the answer in the box.
3:elapsed-duration.stuck: Have the child write both times first. For hours, count the hours on from the first clock: "9 o'clock, 10, 11, 12: three hours." For minutes, count by fives from where the first minute hand points to where the second one points, going past the 12 if it has to.

3:thermometer.say: "A thermometer shows how hot or cold it is. Find where the red line stops on the scale and write that temperature in degrees Fahrenheit."
3:thermometer.first: Look at the scale of the first thermometer together: the numbers go up by tens, and each small mark between two numbers is 2 more degrees. Put a finger on the top of the red line, find the number just below it, and count up by twos to the top of the line. Write the number in the box.
3:thermometer.stuck: Have the child find the number just below the top of the red line and count the small marks up by twos: "80, 82, 84, 86, 88." The top of the red line is the temperature, never the number above it.

K:count-out-n.say: "Look at the number at the start of each row. Color that many pictures in the row, no more and no fewer. Leave the other pictures white."
K:count-out-n.first: Read the first number together. Touch the pictures of that row one by one as the class counts aloud, and color one picture for each number said. Stop at the number. Count the colored pictures once more to check.
K:count-out-n.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the first picture and say "one" while coloring it, then "two" on the next. Stop when the count reaches the number in the circle. If the child has colored too many, count the colored ones together and start a fresh row more slowly.

K:class-rules.say: "Each row shows the same child two times. In one picture the child follows a class rule. Circle that picture, and put an X on the other one."
K:class-rules.first: Do the first row together. Ask, "Which picture keeps everyone safe or helps us learn?" (walking in the hall, raising a hand, listening at story time, cleaning up the blocks). Have the children say the rule in their own words, then circle that picture and cross out the other.
K:class-rules.stuck: Point to each picture and ask, "What is the child doing? Is that what we do in our class?" Say the rule for the child ("We walk in the hall.") and let the child find the picture that shows it.

K:take-turns-share.say: "Look at each picture. If the friends are taking turns, sharing or helping, circle it. If someone is not being kind, put an X on it."
K:take-turns-share.first: Do one picture together. Ask, "What is happening here? Is that kind?" Talk about what the child does, never about a bad child. If a picture shows grabbing, say: "Grabbing a toy is not kind. What could the child do instead?"
K:take-turns-share.stuck: Ask how the other friend in the picture feels: a happy friend usually means a kind picture, a sad friend means someone was not kind. Some pages have more kind pictures than others, so look at each picture on its own.

K:long-ago-today.say: "The pictures on the left are things from long ago. The pictures on the right are things we use today. Draw a line from each long-ago thing to the thing that does the same job today."
K:long-ago-today.first: Name the long-ago things on your page together. Do the top one together: "What job does this do? Which thing on the right does that job today?"
K:long-ago-today.stuck: Ask, "What job does this do?" (washing clothes, giving light at night, getting from place to place, talking to someone far away). Then have the child find the picture on the right that does the same job.

K:community-helpers.say: "Each helper on the left uses one of the tools on the right. Draw a line from each helper to the tool they use."
K:community-helpers.first: Name each helper and each tool on your page together. Do the top helper together: "What does this helper do at work? Which tool helps with that job?" If there is one more tool than helpers, one tool belongs to no one on the page; it gets no line.
K:community-helpers.stuck: Ask, "What does this helper do at work? What do they hold to do it?" Let the child act it out, then find that tool.

K:wants-needs.say: "Draw a line from each picture to Needs or to Wants. Needs are things we must have to live. Wants are things that are nice to have."
K:wants-needs.first: Point to the words Needs and Wants and read them aloud. Do the first picture together: "Can we live without this? Then is it a need or a want?"
K:wants-needs.stuck: Ask, "Could you live without it?" Food, water, clothes and a home are needs; toys and treats are wants.

K:choosing-one-thing.say: "In each row you can have only one thing. Circle the one you choose and put an X on the one you do not pick. There is no wrong answer."
K:choosing-one-thing.first: The small "1" at the start of a row is not a choice. Read the first row together and say what the 1 means: a hand with a coin, "You have one coin. You can buy one of these, not both."; a hand with a book, "You can take home one book."; just the 1, "Recess has time for one thing." Ask, "Which do you choose?" Two children who choose differently are both right.
K:choosing-one-thing.stuck: Ask, "Which one would you like more?" Then help the child put an X on the other one: "That is the one you give up." Check only that every row has one circle and one X.

K:goods-and-services.say: "Each worker on the left makes something or does something. Draw a line from each worker to what they make or do."
K:goods-and-services.first: Name the workers on your page together by what they wear and hold (a tall white hat and a rolling pin: a baker; a hard hat and a hammer: a builder; a striped pole, scissors and a comb: a barber; a cap and a bag of letters: a mail carrier). Do the top worker together: "What does this worker make or do?"
K:goods-and-services.stuck: Ask, "What is this worker holding? What would they make or do with it?"

K:our-flag.say: "This is the flag of our country, the United States. If your flag has red dots, color the stripes with the dots red. Color it like the small flag: red and white stripes, red at the top and the bottom. Color the box blue around the stars, and leave the stars white."
K:our-flag.first: Look at the small colored flag together and name the stripes from the top: red, white, red. Each child needs a red crayon and a blue one; the white stripes and the stars stay white.
K:our-flag.stuck: Have the child put a finger on a stripe of the small flag and find the same stripe on the big one. A stripe colored by mistake is fine; go on to the next stripe together.

K:fair-for-everyone.say: "The two pictures in each row show the same moment. Circle the picture that is fair to everyone."
K:fair-for-everyone.first: Do the first row together. Ask, "In which picture does everyone get a turn, or the same?" Talk about what the children do (keeping the swing, sharing the crackers, letting a friend play), never about a bad child.
K:fair-for-everyone.stuck: Ask how each child in the picture feels. In the fair picture everyone can smile; in the other one someone is left out, still waiting, or has none.

K:hot-cold-places.say: "One big picture is a snowy, cold place and the other is a hot beach. Draw a line from each thing to the place where people would use it."
K:hot-cold-places.first: Name the two places together and ask what the weather is like in each. Do the first thing together: "Would people use this in the snow or at the beach? Why?"
K:hot-cold-places.stuck: Ask, "Would this keep you warm, or help you stay cool?" Things for cold, snowy days go with the snowy place; things for hot, sunny days go with the beach.
